overview.summary: Backtracking is an algorithmic technique for solving problems recursively by trying to build a solution incrementally, one piece at a time, removing those solutions that fail to satisfy the constraints of the problem at any point of time.
learningObjectives: Understand the Choose -> Explore -> Unchoose pattern.
Implement state-reversion to reuse memory across recursive branches.
overview.interviewRelevance: Whenever you see 'Find ALL combinations' or 'Return ALL possible ways', it is 100% a Backtracking problem.

paragraphs: Imagine you are navigating a massive physical maze. You hit an intersection and take the left path. You keep walking until you hit a dead end.
What do you do? You don't teleport back to the start. You walk backwards (backtrack) to that intersection, and try the right path instead.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: Backtracking is just DFS on a tree of possibilities. The magic is in 'cleaning up' your state when you walk backwards so you can try a different path.

definition.technicalDefinition: Backtracking is a general algorithm for finding all (or some) solutions to some computational problems, notably constraint satisfaction problems, that incrementally builds candidates to the solutions, and abandons a candidate ('backtracks') as soon as it determines that the candidate cannot possibly be completed to a valid solution.

vocabulary.definition: The imaginary tree representing all possible decisions.
Stopping the recursion early if you know the current path cannot possibly lead to a valid answer.
Removing the last element added to your temporary path before returning up the call stack.

keyProperties: Time complexity is usually exponential (O(2^N) or O(N!)).

metaphor: A combination lock. You try 0-0-0, then 0-0-1, then 0-0-2. You don't take the lock completely apart; you just spin the last dial. When it reaches 9, you 'backtrack' it to 0 and spin the previous dial.
mentalModel.clickSentence: CHOOSE a decision. EXPLORE it recursively. UNCHOOSE it to clean up. Repeat.

memoryDescription: Backtracking uses a single 'current_path' array to save memory.
Instead of creating a brand new array for every single branch, it modifies the array on the way down, and un-modifies it on the way up.

operations.name: Choose
operations.description: Make a decision. Add the choice to your current state tracking.
operations.visualNote: A node is added to the active path.

operations.name: Explore
operations.description: Recurse deeper into the tree with the new state.

operations.name: Unchoose
operations.description: Undo the decision. Remove the choice from the state so the loop can try the NEXT choice.
operations.visualNote: The node is removed, and the pointer steps back.

patternTemplate.whenToUse: Whenever asked for ALL permutations, combinations, subsets, or solving puzzles like Sudoku/N-Queens.
patternTemplate.timeComplexity: O(2^N) for subsets, O(N!) for permutations.
patternTemplate.spaceComplexity: O(N) for recursion stack and path array.

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: The word 'ALL possible' combined with 'permutations' is a dead giveaway. You must exhaustively explore every combination.

examples.title: Subsets
examples.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set).
steps: Create a backtrack function that takes a start index and current path.
Add a COPY of the current path to the result.
Loop from start index to end of nums.
Add num to path, recurse with index + 1, then pop num from path.
examples.rationale: There are 2^N subsets. For each element, we have a binary choice: include it or don't include it.

conceptQuiz.question: Why MUST we copy the array (e.g., `path[:]` or `[...path]`) before adding it to the final results?
options: Because arrays are passed by reference. If we don't copy it, the final result will just be a list of references to the exact same empty array after all the `.pop()` calls.
Because it makes the code run faster.
To satisfy the compiler's type checker.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If you just do `res.append(path)`, every entry in `res` points to the same object in memory. Since Backtracking pops everything off at the end, your answer will just be `[[], [], []]`.

conceptQuiz.question: What is 'Pruning' in a Backtracking algorithm?
options: Returning early from a branch if you know it cannot possibly be valid, saving time.
Removing duplicates from the final answer.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If you are trying to find combinations that sum to 10, and your current path sums to 15, there is no point exploring deeper. You 'prune' the branch by returning immediately.

practice.title: Permutations
practice.keyInsight: Loop over ALL elements, but skip ones already in the path.

practice.title: Combination Sum
practice.keyInsight: You can reuse elements, so pass `i` down the recursion instead of `i+1`.

practice.title: N-Queens
practice.keyInsight: Classic backtracking. Place a queen, check validity, recurse, remove queen.
